summary: This work proposes a hybrid photonic/CMOS cryogenic controller for superconducting qubits that distributes shared Gaussian and derivative optical pulse templates to 4 K, where local CMOS circuits apply channel-specific amplitude modulation, pulse gating, and hold timing before microwave upconversion. The architecture achieves 0.905 mW per qubit-control channel at N=1000 qubits with $G=16$ local fan-out groups, substantially below full-waveform Cryo-CMOS (3.448 mW) while retaining programmable amplitude calibration after optical distribution.
motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum processors to thousands of control channels requires reducing both room-temperature-to-cryogenic interconnect burden and 4 K power dissipation while preserving channel-specific amplitude calibration for accurate gate fidelity.
method: The hybrid architecture uses room-temperature optical-template generation (Gaussian and derivative envelopes for DRAG control), optical distribution through passive fan-out with active microring modulators per channel, photodetection, and local CMOS for I/Q upconversion and optional sample-and-hold envelope formation for two-qubit gates. Performance is evaluated via post-layout circuit simulations, optical/thermal models, and five-level transmon and coupled-transmon gate-fidelity calculations.
result: Single-qubit XY/DRAG pulses remain below $10^{-3}$ worst-state error; a representative baseband two-qubit envelope achieves $3.19 \times 10^{-4}$ average overlap error after amplitude recalibration, with worst-state error near $10^{-3}$. The 0.905 mW/channel dissipation uses 126 template fibers and four shared LO coaxes for the N=1000 downlink, leaving ~60% margin within a representative 1.5 W 4 K cooling capacity.
